I ask every writer on my team to picture one reader: an investor in another time zone, opening our release at six in the morning, on a phone, in her second language. She will read the first sentence. She may read the second. After that, we have to earn every line. That is why I cut adjectives before anything else. Distinguished, historic and landmark tell her nothing she can use. What she needs are the relationships between facts, and English gives us small words to show them before the fact arrives. Whereas tells her a contrast is coming. Albeit tells her we are about to limit what we just said. In light of tells her the cause. Get those right, and a reader in her second language can follow a complex argument without effort.

Let me make your life easier by explaining how journalists like me actually work. If you tell me something on the record, I can print it and put your name on it. If you tell me something on background, I can use the information, but I will describe you only as a person familiar with the matter. If you want nothing printed at all, you have to say so before you tell me, not after. And if your release is under embargo until six, I will respect that, but only if the embargo is on the email itself. A final piece of advice. When something goes wrong, send a short holding statement early. Silence is what makes a small story big.

I have a rule that annoys everybody I work with. Before I read a draft, I ask the person who wrote it to tell me what it says. Out loud. Without the document in front of them. About a third of the time they cannot do it, and that is the end of the meeting, because a statement nobody can summarise is not a statement. It is a set of paragraphs that survived a committee. The commonest failure is not legal and it is not stylistic. It is that the news has been moved. Somebody has put the context first, because the context feels responsible, and the actual development is now in line four. A journalist reads two lines. Two. If your news is in line four, the story that appears is somebody else's version of it. The second thing is over-qualification. Every reviewer adds one careful word, and each one is defensible on its own, and by the fifth pass the sentence commits to nothing at all. You have to protect the verb. If the verb goes soft, nothing else in the paragraph matters. And the last one, which people find uncomfortable. Decide what you would say if it goes badly, before it goes well. Write the difficult version while everybody is calm. Nobody writes anything sensible at eleven at night with a journalist on the phone, and that is precisely when the drawer gets opened.
